programming.shortDefinition: Programming is the practice of expressing a problem-solving process as precise, testable instructions that a computer can execute and people can maintain.
programming.fullDefinition: Programming combines decomposition, algorithms, data representation, control flow, interfaces, testing, debugging, and maintainability. Knowing syntax is only one layer. Strong programmers clarify requirements, choose appropriate abstractions, reason about failure conditions, verify behavior, and leave code that another person can understand and safely change.
programming.whyItMatters: The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 identifies programming and technological literacy as important differentiators between growing and declining roles, while software and application developers remain among rapidly growing technology occupations. AI changes how code is produced, but not the need to specify, test, review, and maintain software.
realWorldScenarios: A developer converts a vague request into explicit inputs, outputs, constraints, and edge cases before coding.
An analyst writes a small script to make a recurring transformation reproducible instead of repeating spreadsheet steps manually.
A programmer reviews AI-generated code for security, correctness, dependencies, and tests before integrating it.
beginnerActions: Build small programs that use variables, conditions, loops, functions, and basic data structures.
Predict what a short program will do before running it, then compare the result with your reasoning.
When debugging, reduce the problem to the smallest reproducible example.
intermediateActions: Write automated tests for expected behavior and meaningful edge cases.
Refactor a working program to improve naming, structure, duplication, and readability without changing behavior.
Use version control so changes can be inspected, discussed, and reversed.
advancedActions: Design interfaces and abstractions that isolate likely change instead of spreading assumptions throughout a codebase.
Evaluate performance, security, reliability, and maintainability trade-offs before optimizing.
Establish review and testing practices for AI-assisted code generation rather than treating generated code as trusted output.
commonMistakes: Memorizing syntax without learning decomposition and debugging.
Optimizing before correctness and bottlenecks are understood.
Writing code that works only for the happy path.
Adding dependencies for problems that do not require them.
Accepting AI-generated code without understanding or testing it.
programming.evidenceSummary: The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 reports programming as a meaningful differentiator between growing and declining roles and identifies software and application developers among fast-growing technology occupations, while also noting that technological change can both increase and reduce programming demand depending on context.
scholarlyNotes: World Economic Forum (2025), Future of Jobs Report 2025, Skills Outlook. https://www.weforum.org/publications/the-future-of-jobs-report-2025/in-full/3-skills-outlook/
programming.howToMeasureProgress: Measure whether you can translate requirements into working software, diagnose failures systematically, write tests that catch regressions, explain your design decisions, and safely modify unfamiliar code. Shipping more lines of code is not a useful mastery metric.
programming.aiEraRelevance: AI can draft functions, tests, migrations, and explanations rapidly. Programming skill increasingly includes specification, architecture, review, debugging, security judgment, and verification of generated code rather than typing every token manually.

user-experience-design.shortDefinition: User experience design is the evidence-informed practice of shaping products and services so people can understand them, accomplish important goals, recover from errors, and use them effectively in their real context.
user-experience-design.fullDefinition: UX design connects user needs with product behavior. It involves research, problem framing, information architecture, interaction design, prototyping, usability evaluation, accessibility, content decisions, and iteration. Strong UX does not simply make interfaces attractive; it reduces avoidable confusion and friction while balancing user needs with technical, operational, and business constraints.
user-experience-design.whyItMatters: The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 expects design and user experience skills to grow in importance as digital transformation continues. As generating interface variations becomes easier, understanding users and validating whether an experience actually works become more—not less—important.
realWorldScenarios: A designer observes users attempting a task before deciding that the problem needs another feature.
A team prototypes a checkout change and tests whether customers can complete it without explanation.
A designer includes keyboard navigation, readable hierarchy, clear errors, and recovery states as part of the design rather than adding accessibility at the end.
beginnerActions: Choose one user task and map the steps, decisions, information, and likely failure points.
Watch several people attempt a prototype without coaching them through it.
Rewrite one confusing interface message so it explains what happened and what the user can do next.
intermediateActions: Combine interviews or observation with behavioral evidence rather than relying on stated preference alone.
Prototype competing interaction approaches before committing engineering effort.
Evaluate accessibility and usability as design requirements throughout the workflow.
advancedActions: Build research systems that connect recurring user evidence with product decisions and outcomes.
Design coherent experiences across channels, devices, roles, and service touchpoints rather than isolated screens.
Measure whether design changes improve task success, comprehension, error recovery, accessibility, and relevant business outcomes.
commonMistakes: Treating UX as visual styling.
Asking users to design the solution instead of studying their needs and behavior.
Testing only with colleagues who already understand the product.
Using engagement as a proxy for user success without examining the task.
Generating polished AI mockups before the underlying problem is understood.
user-experience-design.evidenceSummary: The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 says design and user experience skills are expected to grow with technological change and digital transformation, while industry demand varies by sector.
scholarlyNotes: World Economic Forum (2025), Future of Jobs Report 2025, Skills Outlook. https://www.weforum.org/publications/the-future-of-jobs-report-2025/in-full/3-skills-outlook/
user-experience-design.howToMeasureProgress: Track whether users can complete important tasks, understand system status, recover from errors, and use the experience across relevant accessibility needs. Strong UX decisions should be traceable to evidence and tested outcomes, not only stakeholder preference.
user-experience-design.aiEraRelevance: AI makes interface generation and prototyping dramatically faster. Human UX skill shifts toward research quality, problem selection, accessibility, behavioral interpretation, system coherence, and deciding which generated experience actually serves users.

information-literacy.shortDefinition: Information literacy is the ability to recognize what information is needed, find appropriate sources, evaluate their credibility and relevance, trace claims to evidence, and use information responsibly.
information-literacy.fullDefinition: Information literacy turns searching into evidence work. It includes framing the information need, selecting source types appropriate to the question, distinguishing primary evidence from commentary, checking authorship and provenance, comparing claims across sources, recognizing uncertainty, and citing or documenting material so others can inspect it. It also includes knowing when available evidence is insufficient.
information-literacy.whyItMatters: Search engines, social platforms, and generative AI can produce plausible answers faster than people can verify them. NIST's Generative AI Profile describes risks involving confidently false or misleading generated content, reinforcing the need for provenance, evaluation, and verification when AI is part of an information workflow.
realWorldScenarios: A researcher follows a statistic from a blog to the original report before using it in an article.
A job seeker distinguishes a company's official hiring information from a reposted listing with outdated details.
An analyst asks an AI assistant for possible sources but opens and checks each source before treating the answer as evidence.
beginnerActions: For one important claim, locate the original or closest available primary source.
Record author, date, source type, and evidence when saving research instead of bookmarking context-free links.
Compare at least two independent sources when a factual claim materially affects a decision.
intermediateActions: Match source type to question—for example, official documentation for product behavior and peer-reviewed or primary research for scientific claims.
Trace citations backward to check whether a secondary source accurately represents the original.
Separate what a source directly establishes from your interpretation or inference.
advancedActions: Design research workflows that preserve provenance from raw source through final claim.
Evaluate conflicting evidence by comparing methods, populations, definitions, incentives, and recency.
Create verification standards for AI-assisted research based on the consequence of being wrong.
commonMistakes: Treating search ranking as a credibility score.
Citing a source that mentions a topic but does not support the actual claim.
Using several articles that all trace back to one original source and calling them independent confirmation.
Ignoring publication date when facts change quickly.
Trusting fabricated or misrepresented AI citations because they look academic.
information-literacy.evidenceSummary: NIST's Generative AI Profile describes risks associated with confabulated or false generated information and emphasizes testing, evaluation, verification, validation, and risk management across AI use. These concerns make source provenance and claim verification central to modern information literacy.
scholarlyNotes: NIST (2024), Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile. https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1
information-literacy.howToMeasureProgress: Measure whether important claims can be traced to suitable evidence, whether source quality matches the stakes of the decision, whether conflicting evidence is handled explicitly, and whether you can identify what remains unknown rather than filling gaps with confidence.
information-literacy.aiEraRelevance: AI makes synthesis fast but can obscure provenance. Information literacy becomes a core human control: users need to inspect sources, distinguish generated explanation from evidence, verify citations, and calibrate trust to consequences.

media-literacy.shortDefinition: Media literacy is the ability to interpret, evaluate, contextualize, and responsibly create media by examining evidence, framing, incentives, provenance, and how a message may shape perception.
media-literacy.fullDefinition: Media literacy goes beyond deciding whether a post is true or false. It considers who created a message, for whom, with what evidence and incentives; how editing, selection, visuals, headlines, algorithms, and format affect interpretation; what context may be missing; and how claims can be checked. It also applies when producing media: creators are responsible for accurate framing and transparent use of synthetic material.
media-literacy.whyItMatters: Digital distribution makes it easy for edited, decontextualized, synthetic, or simply mistaken material to travel quickly. Generative AI further lowers the cost of creating persuasive text, images, audio, and video, increasing the value of provenance and verification skills.
realWorldScenarios: A viewer locates the full interview before judging a short viral clip.
A marketer distinguishes sponsored creator content from independent editorial coverage.
A content producer labels synthetic material where appropriate and verifies factual claims before publishing.
beginnerActions: Before sharing a surprising claim, locate the original source or full context.
Identify whether a piece of media is reporting, analysis, opinion, advertising, satire, or user-generated content.
Check the publication date and whether an old image or story is being presented as current.
intermediateActions: Compare how several outlets frame the same documented event and identify differences in selection and emphasis.
Reverse-trace images, quotations, or clips to their earliest reliable context when provenance matters.
Separate what a piece of media shows directly from the conclusion its caption or narrator asks you to draw.
advancedActions: Create editorial standards for synthetic media, corrections, sourcing, and conflicts of interest.
Analyze how recommendation systems and audience incentives can amplify particular forms of content without assuming amplification proves truth or falsity.
Teach verification through concrete source-tracing exercises rather than generic advice to be skeptical.
commonMistakes: Assuming professional production quality means factual reliability.
Treating all sources as equally credible in the name of balance.
Judging an entire claim from a headline or short clip.
Calling unfamiliar information misinformation without checking it.
Assuming AI-detection tools can reliably establish whether all media is synthetic.
media-literacy.evidenceSummary: NIST's Generative AI Profile identifies risks from synthetic and confabulated content and provides a risk-management framework for generative systems. The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 also expects marketing and media skills to grow with technological change and digital transformation.
scholarlyNotes: NIST (2024), Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile. https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1
World Economic Forum (2025), Future of Jobs Report 2025, Skills Outlook. https://www.weforum.org/publications/the-future-of-jobs-report-2025/in-full/3-skills-outlook/
media-literacy.howToMeasureProgress: Progress shows up when you verify before sharing, recover missing context, distinguish evidence from framing, recognize commercial or algorithmic incentives, and create media whose factual claims and synthetic elements can be explained transparently.
media-literacy.aiEraRelevance: Generative AI expands both legitimate creative possibilities and the supply of convincing synthetic material. Media literacy increasingly requires provenance awareness, contextual verification, and responsible disclosure rather than reliance on visual intuition alone.

data-visualization.shortDefinition: Data visualization is the practice of encoding data visually so that patterns, comparisons, uncertainty, and important exceptions can be understood accurately and efficiently.
data-visualization.fullDefinition: Data visualization begins with the analytical question, not a chart type. It involves choosing appropriate measures and comparisons, selecting visual encodings suited to the task, preserving honest scales and context, reducing irrelevant decoration, labeling clearly, representing uncertainty when it matters, and testing whether the intended audience can interpret the display correctly.
data-visualization.whyItMatters: Charts can reveal patterns that are difficult to see in tables, but they can also exaggerate, hide, or imply relationships. As AI and analytics tools make chart production easier, the scarce capability becomes deciding what should be shown and whether the visual supports an accurate interpretation.
realWorldScenarios: An analyst uses a line chart to show a time trend and annotates the policy change that affects interpretation.
A marketer shows both conversion rate and the underlying number of visitors so a percentage is not detached from scale.
A researcher includes uncertainty around an estimate rather than presenting a single precise point as certainty.
beginnerActions: State the question a chart should answer before selecting the visual form.
Use direct labels, units, time periods, and meaningful comparison points.
Remove visual elements that do not help the reader interpret the data.
intermediateActions: Choose encodings based on the task: comparison, distribution, relationship, composition, geography, or change over time.
Check whether axis choices, aggregation, or missing values materially alter the apparent pattern.
Test a visualization with someone unfamiliar with the analysis and ask what conclusion they draw.
advancedActions: Design interactive or multi-view displays that preserve context while allowing useful exploration.
Represent uncertainty and data quality without overwhelming the primary message.
Create visualization standards that prevent recurring misleading practices across a reporting system.
commonMistakes: Choosing a chart because it looks impressive rather than because it fits the question.
Truncating scales in ways that exaggerate ordinary differences.
Using too many colors, categories, or dimensions at once.
Showing percentages without counts or relevant baselines.
Accepting an AI-generated chart without checking calculations, labels, aggregation, and source data.
data-visualization.howToMeasureProgress: Measure whether readers can identify the intended pattern accurately, whether the display preserves important context and uncertainty, and whether visual choices survive scrutiny when the underlying data and transformations are inspected.
data-visualization.aiEraRelevance: AI can generate visualizations from natural language, but it may choose poor encodings or mis-handle data. Human skill remains essential for defining the analytical question, validating transformations, detecting misleading displays, and communicating uncertainty.

automation.shortDefinition: Automation is the design of systems that perform repeatable work with reduced manual intervention while preserving appropriate controls, observability, exception handling, and human accountability.
automation.fullDefinition: Useful automation begins by understanding the process. It identifies stable inputs, rules, outputs, dependencies, exceptions, permissions, and failure consequences before selecting a tool. Strong automation includes monitoring, logs, retries or fallback behavior, ownership, and a way for people to intervene. Automating a poor process can make its problems faster and less visible.
automation.whyItMatters: The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 identifies robotics and automation, AI, and expanding digital access as major drivers of job and skill transformation through 2030. Workers increasingly need to decide which tasks should be automated and how automated workflows should fail safely.
realWorldScenarios: A marketing team automatically routes form submissions into a CRM but flags incomplete or suspicious records for review.
An operations team automates a recurring report only after standardizing definitions and source data.
A developer adds monitoring and a manual override to an AI agent that can take external actions.
beginnerActions: Map one repetitive workflow and identify its trigger, inputs, rules, output, and exceptions.
Automate a low-risk deterministic step before attempting an end-to-end autonomous workflow.
Document how to stop or bypass the automation when it behaves incorrectly.
intermediateActions: Add validation, logging, alerts, retries, and exception queues appropriate to the workflow.
Measure whether automation actually reduces cycle time, errors, or effort after maintenance costs are included.
Review permissions and data exposure for every connected service.
advancedActions: Design human-in-the-loop controls based on the consequence and reversibility of errors.
Create idempotent or recoverable workflows where repeated execution could otherwise create damage.
Audit automated decisions for drift, hidden dependencies, and failure patterns after deployment.
commonMistakes: Automating before simplifying the process.
Assuming the happy path represents the real workflow.
Creating automations with no owner or monitoring.
Giving integrations unnecessarily broad permissions.
Using autonomous AI for irreversible high-impact actions without appropriate review.
automation.evidenceSummary: The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 identifies robotics and autonomous systems, AI and information processing, and broader digital access as major forces reshaping jobs and skill demand through 2030.
scholarlyNotes: World Economic Forum (2025), Future of Jobs Report 2025. https://www.weforum.org/publications/the-future-of-jobs-report-2025/
NIST (2024), Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile. https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1
automation.howToMeasureProgress: Track end-to-end time, error rates, manual intervention, exception volume, recovery time, maintenance burden, and whether the automation's permissions and behavior remain appropriate as the process changes.
automation.aiEraRelevance: AI expands automation from fixed rules toward probabilistic interpretation and action. That increases the need for evaluation, observability, scoped permissions, escalation, and human control when outputs are uncertain or consequences are significant.

ai-evaluation.shortDefinition: AI evaluation is the systematic practice of testing whether an AI system performs acceptably for a defined use case, including its quality, reliability, failure modes, risks, and behavior under realistic conditions.
ai-evaluation.fullDefinition: AI evaluation starts by defining what good performance means for a specific task and what failures matter. It then uses representative examples, baselines, metrics, human judgment where appropriate, adversarial or edge cases, and repeated testing to characterize behavior. Evaluation continues after deployment because models, prompts, data, users, and surrounding systems can change.
ai-evaluation.whyItMatters: Generative systems can produce fluent outputs that are difficult to assess by appearance alone. NIST's AI Risk Management resources emphasize testing, evaluation, verification, and validation as part of trustworthy AI risk management, making evaluation a practical capability for teams deploying AI-enabled workflows.
realWorldScenarios: A support team builds a set of real customer questions and expected qualities before comparing AI assistants.
A researcher measures citation correctness separately from writing quality because fluent prose can still contain unsupported claims.
A product team tests an agent's behavior when tools fail, permissions are missing, or instructions conflict.
beginnerActions: Define the task and write down what a successful output must and must not do.
Create a small evaluation set containing ordinary examples and obvious edge cases.
Compare the AI workflow with a meaningful baseline rather than judging it in isolation.
intermediateActions: Separate evaluation dimensions such as factuality, relevance, completeness, safety, latency, and cost where they matter.
Use blind human review when subjective quality is important and feasible.
Record failures by category so prompt, data, model, tool, and workflow problems can be distinguished.
advancedActions: Build repeatable evaluation pipelines that run when models, prompts, retrieval, tools, or policies change.
Use risk-based test coverage so high-consequence failure modes receive deeper evaluation.
Monitor deployed systems for drift and collect representative failures back into the evaluation set.
commonMistakes: Testing only a few hand-picked examples.
Using the same model to generate and unquestioningly grade its own answers.
Optimizing one metric while ignoring consequential failure modes.
Changing prompts or models without regression testing.
Assuming a benchmark score proves suitability for a specific real-world workflow.
ai-evaluation.evidenceSummary: NIST's AI Resource Center and Generative AI Profile emphasize testing, evaluation, verification, and validation as practical components of trustworthy AI risk management across the AI lifecycle.
scholarlyNotes: NIST (2024), Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile. https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1
NIST AI Resource Center, Testing, Evaluation, Verification and Validation resources. https://airc.nist.gov/
ai-evaluation.howToMeasureProgress: Progress means evaluations become representative, repeatable, tied to actual consequences, and useful for detecting regressions. A mature team can explain not only average performance but important failure modes and the conditions under which human review is required.
ai-evaluation.aiEraRelevance: Evaluation is one of the defining AI-era skills because model capability is probabilistic and context-dependent. Teams that can test systems rigorously can adopt new models faster without confusing impressive demonstrations with dependable performance.
